items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 4 "Infer": Why have models of the solar system changed over the centuries?

body.html: A model is a tool for explaining the evidence we have. When new observations show something the old model cannot explain, the model must be revised or replaced.

Early models placed Earth at the center, with the Sun and planets circling it. Careful observations of planetary motion, and later the telescope, showed moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus, which the Earth-centered model could not explain. The Sun-centered model explained them, and later measurements refined it again (elliptical orbits instead of circles).

answer.html: Models change because new observations and better instruments provide evidence that the older model cannot explain, so scientists refine or replace it.

check.html: A model that ignored contradicting evidence would stop being scientific.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 7): Explain how a plastic model of the human heart, used in a health class, is helpful.

body.html: A model lets us study things that are too large, too small, too slow, or too hazardous to observe directly.

A real beating heart is hidden inside the body and cannot be handled or taken apart safely. The plastic model can be held, opened, and labeled, so students can see the chambers and valves and how blood flows through them.

answer.html: The model makes a hidden, delicate system visible and easy to examine, so students can study its parts without harming anyone.

check.html: It fits the reasons for using models: the real thing is hard or unsafe to examine directly.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 5 "Identify": Identify models you might find in a science museum.

body.html: Typical museum models: a scale model of a dinosaur skeleton, a planetarium dome showing the night sky, a working model of a steam engine, a diagram of a food web, a computer simulation of a tornado, and a plastic model of DNA.

answer.html: A dinosaur skeleton replica, a planetarium projection, a DNA model, and a tornado simulation are all models.

check.html: Each one represents something real in a simpler or more convenient form.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 8): Discuss how computer simulations can help city planners develop possible solutions to a traffic problem.

body.html: Simulations let designers test different solutions quickly, cheaply, and safely.

A traffic simulation lets planners change one variable at a time (the timing of signals, the number of lanes, a new roundabout) and watch how long cars wait. They can compare many designs without closing a single road, test rare conditions such as a stadium crowd leaving at once, and show the public how the best design will perform.

answer.html: Simulations let planners test and compare many possible solutions without disrupting real traffic, so they can choose the design that works best before spending money to build it.

check.html: Matches the idea that simulations are fast, cheap, and safe ways to try designs.

items.title: Lesson 1, Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Poster on a model not mentioned in the lesson

body.html: A model represents a system so that a process can be tested. A model does not have to be physical.

Example: a computer model of a hurricane's path. Type: computer (mathematical) model. It uses ocean temperature, wind speed, and air pressure data to predict where the storm will go, which cannot be tested by sending people into a real storm. Evidence: the predicted track is compared with the track the storm actually follows; agreement supports the model, and disagreement tells forecasters what to revise.

answer.html: Model: a computer model of a hurricane's path. It lets forecasters test how conditions affect the storm's track, and it is supported by agreement between predicted and observed tracks.

check.html: This is a project; any well-supported model is acceptable.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 1: A student wants to find out whether plants grow taller under blue light than under red light. Summarize the steps of the investigation using scientific methods.

body.html: The usual sequence (not rigid) is state the problem, gather information, form a hypothesis, test it, analyze the data, draw conclusions, and share the work for review.

Problem: does light color affect plant height? Research: read about how plants use light. Hypothesis: "Plants under blue light will grow taller than plants under red light." Test: grow identical seedlings (same soil, water, and temperature) under each color, with a control group in white light, and measure heights every day. Analyze: graph height versus time for each group. Conclude: if the blue-light plants are taller, the data support the hypothesis; if not, modify it. Share the results with other students or scientists for review.

answer.html: State the problem, research it, form a hypothesis, test it with a controlled experiment, analyze the data, draw conclusions (modify the hypothesis or repeat the tests if needed), and have others review the work.

check.html: Only one variable (light color) changes between groups, so the test is fair.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 2: Define hypothesis, then identify three ways to test the hypothesis "Heavier toy cars roll farther down a ramp."

body.html: A hypothesis is a possible explanation for a problem, based on what you know and have observed, that can be tested. Three ways to test this one: (1) make observations, such as watching many cars of different masses roll down playground slides and ramps; (2) build a model, such as a computer simulation of a car on a ramp with friction, and compare it with real cars; (3) perform an experiment with a control, rolling cars of different masses down the same ramp from the same starting point and measuring how far each goes.

answer.html: A hypothesis is a testable possible explanation for an observed problem. This one could be tested by observation, by building a model, or by a controlled experiment that changes only the car's mass.

check.html: All three methods can produce data that agree or disagree with the hypothesis.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 3: A lab partner throws away one of five trials because it "doesn't fit." Why is it important to avoid bias?

body.html: Bias occurs when a scientist's expectations affect which data are kept or how results are interpreted. Throwing out a trial only because it disagrees with what was expected makes the conclusion look better than the evidence allows, and others who repeat the experiment will not get the same result.

answer.html: Bias can lead scientists to select or interpret results to match what they expected, which gives misleading conclusions. Avoiding it (keeping every trial, taking accurate notes, running enough trials, and having others review) keeps results honest and reproducible.

check.html: Keeping all trials and explaining outliers is the remedy named in the text.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 4: Why do scientists use models? Give an example of a model different from the ones in this lesson.

body.html: Scientists use models when what they study is too large, too small, takes too long to see, or is hazardous. Example: a computer model of how a virus attaches to a human cell. The virus is far too small to see directly, and the model lets researchers test how different shapes would fit.

answer.html: Models represent things that are too large, too small, too slow, or too dangerous to study directly. Example: a computer model of a virus attaching to a cell lets researchers study something too small to see.

check.html: The example is not one used in the lesson, and it fits the "too small" reason.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 5: A poll of 40 students leaving the band room finds that 85 percent say jazz is the best kind of music. The poll taker concludes that everyone in the school thinks jazz is the best. Evaluate the conclusion.

body.html: A survey of opinions measures preferences in a sample; it cannot prove a statement about everyone. An opinion about which music is "best" is not testable by science.

The sample is only students in the band room, who are probably more interested in music than the typical student. Even 85% leaves 15% who disagree. What is "best" is a matter of taste, so no experiment can settle it.

answer.html: The poll shows that most of the 40 students polled prefer jazz, but it does not prove that everyone does. The sample is limited and biased, 15% disagreed, and whether music is "best" is an opinion that science cannot prove.

check.html: 85% is not 100%, so "everyone" is false even for the students polled.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 6: The accepted density of aluminum is 2.70 g/cm³. In your lab you measure 2.52 g/cm³. Should the accepted value be thrown out?

body.html: The accepted value comes from many careful measurements by many experimenters. Your single experiment differs by 0.18 g/cm³. Compute the percent difference.
An error of several percent is common in a classroom measurement (volume reading, trapped air bubbles, balance zero). The likely cause is experimental error, not a wrong accepted value.

answer.html: No. One experiment that differs by 6.7% is far less convincing than many repeated, carefully checked measurements. Look for sources of error in your procedure (how the volume was measured, the balance zero) and repeat the experiment.

check.html: 6.7% is a reasonable difference for a first classroom measurement.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 4 "Infer": Why have models of the atom changed over the years?

body.html: A model is a tool for explaining current evidence. When new experiments give evidence the old model cannot explain, the model must be revised or replaced.

Thomson's "plum pudding" model could not explain later experimental results. Rutherford's results led to a compact nucleus with orbiting electrons. Later discoveries (the nucleus contains protons and neutrons, electrons behave like a cloud) produced the present model.

answer.html: Models change because new observations and technologies provide new evidence that the older model cannot explain, so scientists refine or replace it.

check.html: A model that never changed despite new contradicting evidence would not be scientific.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 7): Explain how the model shown at the beginning of this module is helpful.

body.html: The picture shows students studying a model of the solar system. A model lets us study things that are too big, too slow, or too far away to observe directly.

The real solar system is billions of kilometers across and its planets take years to orbit. A small model lets students see relative sizes, positions, and motions at once, take notes, and make predictions.

answer.html: The model shrinks a system that is too large (and too slow-moving) to observe directly into one that can be seen and studied in a classroom.

check.html: It matches the book's reasons for models: too large, too small, too slow, or hazardous.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 5 "Identify": Identify other models around your classroom.

body.html: Models in a typical classroom: a globe (Earth), a periodic table (organizes elements), a skeleton or atom kit, a wall map, a physical demonstration of a molecule, a graph or equation on the board, or a computer simulation.

answer.html: A globe, a ball-and-stick molecule kit, a wall map, a graph on the board, and a computer simulation are all models.

check.html: Each one represents something real in a simpler, more usable form.

items.title: Lesson 1, "Get It?" (page 8): Discuss how computer simulations can help develop possible solutions to a problem.

body.html: From the text: simulations let engineers test different designs quickly, cheaply, and safely.

A simulation lets you change one variable at a time (wing shape, bridge material), see which design is most efficient or economical, test dangerous conditions without risk (a flight simulator with a storm), and show a client how the design will perform.

answer.html: Simulations let designers test and compare many possible solutions safely and cheaply before building anything real, and they help present the best design to others.

check.html: Matches the flight-simulator example in the text.

items.title: Lesson 1, Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Poster on a model not mentioned in the lesson

body.html: A model represents a system so a process can be tested. It does not have to be physical.

Example: a mathematical model of a car's stopping distance (distance = speed × reaction time + braking distance). Type: mathematical/computer model. It tests how speed changes stopping distance without crashing real cars. Evidence: the model's predictions can be compared with measured stopping distances on a test track; agreement supports the model, disagreement tells us what to revise.

answer.html: Model: a mathematical model of stopping distance. It lets us test how speed and road conditions affect stopping, and it is supported by agreement between predicted and measured stopping distances.

check.html: This is a project; any well-supported model is acceptable.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 1: Summarize the steps of an investigation using scientific methods

body.html: Figure 2 and the text list the usual sequence (not rigid).

State the problem → research and gather information → form a hypothesis → test the hypothesis (experiment or observation) → analyze the data → draw conclusions → peer review. If the data do not support the hypothesis, modify the hypothesis; if they do, repeat the test several times.

answer.html: State the problem, gather information, form a hypothesis, test it, analyze the data, draw conclusions (modify the hypothesis or repeat the tests as needed), and have peers review the work.

check.html: Steps follow the flow chart in Figure 2.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 2: Define hypothesis; identify three ways to test it

body.html: A hypothesis is a possible explanation for a problem, based on what you know and have observed, that can be tested. The text names ways to test: (1) making observations, (2) building a model and relating it to real-life situations, (3) performing an experiment with a control.

answer.html: A hypothesis is a testable possible explanation for an observed problem. It can be tested by observation, by building a model, or by performing a controlled experiment.

check.html: Includes the three methods from the text.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 3: Why is it important to avoid bias?

body.html: Bias occurs when a scientist's expectations affect how results are analyzed or what conclusions are drawn (for example, keeping only the trial that agrees with expectations). That produces unreliable conclusions that others cannot reproduce.

answer.html: Bias can lead scientists to select or interpret results to fit what they expected, which gives misleading conclusions. Avoiding it (more trials, accurate notes, peer review) keeps results honest and reproducible.

check.html: Links to the text's remedies: many trials and accurate notes.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 4: Why do scientists use models? Give a new example.

body.html: Scientists use models when what they study is too large, too small, takes too long to see, or is hazardous. Example: a wind tunnel model of an airplane is a physical model; it lets engineers measure airflow over a design much smaller (and cheaper and safer) than a full aircraft.

answer.html: Models represent things that are too large, too small, too slow, or too dangerous to study directly. Example: a scale model of an airplane in a wind tunnel shows how air flows over the design before the full-size plane is built.

check.html: The example is not one used in the lesson (atom models, flight simulator).

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 5: "90 percent of students like pizza, so everyone does"

body.html: A survey of opinions measures preferences of a sample; it cannot prove a statement about everyone. Taste is an opinion and not testable.
The sample is only students in the cafeteria (probably biased toward people who eat pizza there). Even 90% leaves 10% who do not like it. Opinions are outside what science can verify.

answer.html: The survey shows that most of the surveyed students like pizza, but it does not prove everyone does. The sample is limited, 10% disagree, and whether food tastes good is an opinion, not something science can prove for everyone.

check.html: 90% is not 100%, so "everyone" is false even for the sample.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 6: Should the accepted value 9.8 m/s² be tossed out because of your pendulum result of 9.4 m/s²?

body.html: The accepted value comes from many careful measurements by many experimenters. Your single experiment differs by about 0.4 m/s². Compute the difference.

An error of about 4% is typical of simple pendulum experiments (timing, measuring length, small-angle approximation). The likely cause is experimental error in your measurements, not a wrong accepted value.

answer.html: No. One experiment with a few percent error is much less convincing than many repeated, carefully checked measurements. Look for sources of error in your procedure (timing, length measurement) and repeat the experiment.

check.html: 4.1% is a small difference for a classroom experiment.
